Imaging shows an eccentrically located, expansile lytic lesion in the distal femur with cortical thinning and a classic "soap-bubble" appearance and a thin rim of bone; MRI shows a well-demarcated, noninvasive lesion. These features localize to the epiphyseal/metaphyseal region around the knee and are most characteristic of a giant cell tumor (osteoclastoma) in skeletally mature patients (age 20–40). Other possibilities (aneurysmal bone cyst, chondroblastoma, simple bone cyst, infection, malignancy) are less likely given the patient’s age, lesion location, radiographic soap-bubble appearance, and benign-appearing MRI. Mild ESR elevation can be nonspecific. Overall the clinical and imaging pattern best fits a giant cell tumor of the distal femur.

DIAGNOSIS: Giant cell tumor (osteoclastoma) of the distal femur.
